“You may be certain they were all perfectly at ease.”

“Perhaps that would not make me like them any better. So many women and children have no business being comfortable aboard.”

“My dear Frederick, what nonsense you are talking! Tell me, what would become of us unfortunate sailors' wives, so often needing passage from one port to another to follow our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“You see that my feelings did not stop me carrying Mrs. Harville and her entire family to Plymouth.”

“But I dislike hearing you speak like some fine gentleman, as though women were all delicate ladies rather than reasonable beings. None of us looks to sail in smooth water all her life.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “he will change his tune once he has a wife. When he marries, if we are fortunate enough to see another war, we shall find him doing just what you and I, and many others, have done. He will be grateful indeed to anyone who brings his wife to him.”

“Indeed he will.”

“Then I have finished,” Captain Wentworth exclaimed. “Once married people begin upon me with ‘Oh, you will think quite otherwise when you marry,’ all I can answer is ‘No, I shall not.’ Then they repeat ‘Yes, you will,’ and the discussion is over.”

He rose and went away.

“You must have travelled a great deal, ma'am!” Mrs. Musgrove said to Mrs. Croft.

“A fair amount, ma'am, during fifteen years of marriage, although plenty of women have travelled farther. I have crossed the Atlantic four times and gone once to the East Indies and back—only once—besides visiting places nearer home, such as Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I have never passed beyond the Straits, nor been to the West Indies. We do not count Bermuda or Bahama as the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs. Musgrove had no objection to offer; she could not recall ever having called them anything in her life.

“And I assure you, ma'am,” Mrs. Croft went on, “that no accommodations can surpass those of a man-of-war; naturally I mean the higher rates. A frigate, of course, provides less room, although any sensible woman can be quite content in one. I may safely declare that the happiest portion of my life has been passed on a ship. So long as we were together, you understand, there was nothing to dread.

But how could I, a bewildered village boy, avoid that extraordinary contradiction into which even the best and wisest men fall every day?

“All of that may be true,” I told Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

At that, I rolled onto my face, grabbed the hair on both sides of my head, and pulled it hard. All the while I knew how absurd and misplaced my heart's madness was. I felt quite certain that my face would have deserved it if I had lifted my head by the hair and struck it against the pebbles, as punishment for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy, the wisest of girls, stopped trying to reason with me. Her hand was comforting despite its roughness from work. She laid it on each of my hands in turn and gently drew them out of my hair. Then she patted my shoulder softly to soothe me, while I cried a little into my sleeve, exactly as I had in the brewery yard. I had a vague conviction that someone, or perhaps everyone—I couldn't say which—was treating me very badly.

“I'm glad of one thing,” Biddy said. “You felt you could trust me with your secret, Pip. And I'm glad of something else: of course you know you can rely on me to keep it and always deserve your trust that far. If your first teacher—dear me, such a poor teacher, needing so much teaching herself!—were still teaching you now, she thinks she knows the lesson she'd choose. But it would be difficult to learn, and you've moved beyond her, so there's no use in it now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy stood up from the bank. Then, brightening her voice pleasantly, she asked, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, getting up, putting an arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I'll always tell you everything.”

“Until you're a gentleman,” Biddy said.

“You know I'll never be one, so that means always. Not that I really need to tell you anything. You already know everything I know, as I said at home the other night.”

“Ah,” Biddy whispered, looking away towards the ships. Then she repeated, with the same pleasant change of tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told her we should walk farther, and we did. The summer afternoon softened into a summer evening, and it was beautiful.

“What is it?” Oliver asked.

“Quiet!” the Dodger answered. “See that old fellow at the book-stall?”

“The old gentleman across the street?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He'll serve,” said the Dodger.

“A capital plant,” remarked Master Charley Bates.

Oliver glanced between them in the utmost astonishment, but had no opportunity to question them. The two boys slipped across the road and crept up close behind the old gentleman they had pointed out. Oliver followed for a few steps, then stopped, uncertain whether to go forward or turn back, and watched in silent wonder.

The gentleman was a most respectable-looking figure, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar and white trousers, and held an elegant bamboo cane beneath his arm. Having picked up a volume from the stall, he stood reading as intently as though seated in his own armchair in his study. Indeed, he may well have imagined himself there, for his absorption made it clear that neither stall, street, boys, nor anything else existed for him except the book. He was reading it steadily through, turning the leaf whenever he reached the bottom of a page, starting at the first line of the next, and proceeding with the liveliest interest and eagerness.

Imagine Oliver's terror and dismay as, standing a few paces away with his eyes stretched as wide as possible, he saw the Dodger thrust a hand into the gentleman's pocket and extract a handkerchief! Then saw him pass it to Charley Bates! And finally watched both boys dash round the corner at their utmost speed!

In a flash, the whole secret of the handkerchiefs, watches, jewels, and the Jew burst upon the boy's understanding.

For an instant he remained still, terror sending the blood tingling through every vein until he seemed to stand in a blaze. Then, bewildered and afraid, he fled; scarcely knowing what he was doing, he ran as fast as his legs would carry him.

The entire business occupied no more than a minute. At the very moment Oliver started running, the old gentleman put his hand into his pocket, discovered the missing handkerchief, and wheeled round. Seeing the boy hurry away at such speed, he naturally took him for the thief. Crying “Stop thief!” at the top of his voice, he set off in pursuit, still carrying the book.
